{"id": "16:96/q14", "question": "What special reward is promised for patience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q14/p1", "position": "Patient people receive divine recompense, with their bad deeds overlooked or forgiven.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī mention pardon; Ibn Kathīr speaks of overlooking worse deeds. Ibn Jubayr says best worldly deeds are rewarded and bad deeds forgiven. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says 39:10 promises reward without reckoning over deficiencies."}, {"id": "16:96/q14/p2", "position": "The reward includes God's contentment and the desired spiritual outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits Abū ʿUthmān's claim that God grants contentment, with best reward in both lives. Al-Qushayrī says outcomes vary: hardship for God receives immense recompense (39:10), restraining desire receives the chamber (25:75), and acceptance of decree receives divine companionship (2:153)."}, {"id": "16:96/q14/p3", "position": "Patience leads to ample reward and divine presence and love.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 2:177, 33:35, 2:153, 2:249, 8:46, 3:146, 25:75, 28:54, and 39:10 for patience as integral to piety and abundantly rewarded."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q15", "question": "What does ajr mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether ajr is used for divine recompense here or in its wider lexical senses.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q15/p1", "position": "It is reward or recompense for obedience and patience.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī also glosses the Prophet's reward as thawāb at 10:72; Ibn al-Jawzī lists reward for obedience as a Qurʾānic sense. Al-Ālūsī specifies reward corresponding to this patience."}, {"id": "16:96/q15/p2", "position": "The root also denotes a contracted wage, setting a bone, and certain roof terms.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī explains a wage for use of benefits or an act; he also lists setting a bone, ijār for an unenclosed roof, plurals ajājīr and ajājirah, and variant injār."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q16", "question": "How does ajrahum function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether jazā is parsed as taking one direct object here or as a two-object verb of giving.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q16/p1", "position": "It is the direct object of the rewarding verb.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls it the direct object of lanajziyanna."}, {"id": "16:96/q16/p2", "position": "It is the second object of yujziyan when that verb means 'to give.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr analyzes the two-object construction."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q17", "question": "What does the bāʾ in bi-aḥsani express?", "turns_on": "Whether the bāʾ denotes the basis of exchange or the cause of reward.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q17/p1", "position": "It marks recompense or equivalence: reward in exchange for deeds.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares 'I sold this for that.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya says reward is in proportion to the best works."}, {"id": "16:96/q17/p2", "position": "It marks cause: reward because of the exceptionally good deed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links it to remaining Muslim under persecution and cites 12:33."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q18", "question": "What does 'the best of what they used to do' mean for the reward?", "turns_on": "Whether 'best' identifies a class of deeds, a comparative scale of reward, patience itself, or an emphatic way to promise full recompense.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q18/p1", "position": "It refers to obedient acts, especially obligations and recommended works, rather than merely permitted acts.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī say merely permissible acts earn no promised reward. Al-Ṭabrisī takes the comparative as evidence that some good is better than other good. Al-Ālūsī reports an extension to avoiding prohibited and disliked acts, but records al-Irshād's objection that this constricts mercy; Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that permissible good acts are unrelated to this patience."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p2", "position": "It is patience itself, the best act needed by every obligation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers this because patience underlies all duties. Al-Ālūsī reports an implied genitive: reward for their patience."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p3", "position": "God gives every deed the reward of its best instance, elevating even lesser instances.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says divine generosity raises lesser deeds to the level of best deeds. Al-Ālūsī reports that even a lowest-ranked act gets the highest reward, absorbing momentary distress into beautiful patience. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers best-instance recompense for each kind of deed, even if the performed act was not its best instance; he rejects sorting out and discarding merely good works."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p4", "position": "The reward is better than the deeds themselves, multiplied by God.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī offers this alternative; al-Ālūsī reports a parse with an omitted reward qualified by aḥsan and a comparative genitive. Kuranyolu also says reward exceeds the deeds."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p5", "position": "The best works are voluntary acts, chosen freely rather than imposed.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this reason. Al-Ālūsī adds that rewarding them would entail obligatory works, but calls the interpretation entirely unsound; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says obligations have greater merit."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p6", "position": "Aḥsan keeps its comparative force: reward of the best implies reward of lesser good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn prefers this implication by agreement and rejects denial of comparison as a mistaken attempt to avoid it."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p7", "position": "Aḥsan means good without comparative force, or praises excellence without limiting reward.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the noncomparative reading. Bursevī calls it completeness of goodness, citing 3:148. Al-Ālūsī reports al-Irshād's view that the superlative encourages and praises reward, with a parallel in 16:89. Al-Samīn rejects a noncomparative analysis motivated by limiting reward."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p8", "position": "The mention of the best encourages action although reward covers both good and better deeds.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this distinct exhortative reading."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p9", "position": "Aḥsan intensifies the especially good act of remaining Muslim under persecution.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the superlative intensively, with causal bāʾ, and cites 12:33."}, {"id": "16:96/q18/p10", "position": "Only each person's best deeds are rewarded, while merely good deeds are discarded.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī attributes and rejects this proposal because context, reward verses, and divine mercy oppose it."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q19", "question": "What incident is reported around these verses?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in names, property claimed, timing, and what Imruʾ al-Qays did afterward.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q19/p1", "position": "A Kindah–Hadramawt land dispute led to a demanded oath and revelation as Imruʾ al-Qays prepared to swear.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports the claimant lacked proof, the Prophet ordered an oath and warned of God's anger for seizing Muslim property falsely; al-Ashʿath assigned the verses to the two men. Imruʾ al-Qays then acknowledged that his property perishes and his opponent gains reward."}, {"id": "16:96/q19/p2", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAbbās al-Kindī and ʿAbdān ibn Ashrāʾ al-Ḥaḍramī's judgment of a claim to land and a house.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives these names and the land-and-house claim."}, {"id": "16:96/q19/p3", "position": "It concerned Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis and ʿAydān ibn Ashwaʿ over land; as he prepared to swear, he wept and admitted the other's right.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports this from al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "16:96/q19/p4", "position": "After the covenant verses were recited, Imruʾ al-Qays admitted taking land and offered it back with compensation for its fruit; 16:97 then descended about him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports the sequel and its link to the next verse."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q20", "question": "How does the contrast explain the preceding promise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q20/p1", "position": "It explains 16:95: God's promised good is better because enduring divine gifts outlast human gain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a concluding restatement, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī an explanation of the earlier claim. Al-Bayḍāwī says the inexhaustible mercy explains the prior judgment; Study Quran compares 20:131, 28:60, and 42:36. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also cites 28:60 elsewhere."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q21", "question": "Why does the passage move from covenant keeping to patient people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q21/p1", "position": "Keeping a covenant under pressure requires patience, so the promise expands to patient believers generally.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains the shift; Ibn ʿĀshūr says refusing the polytheists' immediate offer calls for endurance. Al-Ālūsī says the emphasized clause repeats the earlier promise to encourage steadfastness."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q22", "question": "What practical choice does the verse urge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q22/p1", "position": "Choose lasting divine reward over worldly gain, and keep faith, covenants, and oaths.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī urges work for what lasts; Abū Mūsā reports the Prophet saying love of either world harms the other, so prefer the enduring. Al-Rāzī says awareness of loss spoils even noble worldly enjoyment. Ibn ʿĀshūr urges reliance on God's promise instead of human offers. Al-Wāḥidī warns against false oaths. Bursevī says faithfulness benefits both lives."}, {"id": "16:96/q22/p2", "position": "The contrast is a general, exceptionless principle with many applications.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses absolute wording, and Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the address proverb-like."}]}

{"id": "16:96/q24", "question": "Which prophetic stories illustrate the patience promised here?", "turns_on": "Which prophet's form of endurance is used as an example.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q24/p1", "position": "Jacob endures Joseph's absence with patience.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 12:18 and 12:83–86 as recurrent examples and reward."}, {"id": "16:96/q24/p2", "position": "Job faithfully endures affliction.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 21:83–84 and 38:41, 44, identifying Job with prophetic steadfastness."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q25", "question": "How do these verses fit the sūrah and its revelation?", "turns_on": "The notes range from revelation classification to the sūrah's theme and nearby wording.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q25/p1", "position": "Verses 95–97, with verse 112, are classified as Madinan by some authorities.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes the classification to Āl and IJ."}, {"id": "16:96/q25/p2", "position": "The sūrah answers objections meant to unsettle the public about the Qurʾān and the Prophet.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī gives this larger purpose."}, {"id": "16:96/q25/p3", "position": "Nearby glad tidings fit the promise of a good life and full reward.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī relates the mention of bushrā to the nearby promise and distinguishes grouped wording in the verse about the Book's clarification, citing 16:89."}, {"id": "16:96/q25/p4", "position": "The prior warning's singular indefinite 'foot' heightens danger: one person's slip implies the danger of many.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf connects the nearby foot image with slipping from truth after firmness."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q01", "question": "Who is the seeker of the immediate life?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning is restricted to unbelief and a sole life goal, or extends to people doing ostensibly religious deeds for worldly ends; everlasting Hell and the contrast with 17:19 are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q01/p1", "position": "One devoted to this world alone, denying or neglecting the Hereafter; the warning especially concerns unbelievers.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā identifies an idolater without belief in the Hereafter. Ṭabarī describes no belief in resurrection or hope of divine reward or punishment. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn Jarīr restrict the warning to unbelievers. Abū Ḥayyān infers the omitted contrast from 17:19. Al-Ālūsī argues everlasting Hell requires an unbeliever, although banishment can describe a believer's time in Hell. Ibn ʿĀshūr says worldly desire rests on seeing no life after death. Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows denial in deeds despite verbal acknowledgment."}, {"id": "17:18/q01/p2", "position": "The seeker includes anyone who directs deeds or apparent devotion toward worldly gain, including hypocrites, show-offs, sinners, migrants, and fighters seeking spoils or fame.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf distinguishes ordinary worldly pursuit from afterlife deeds done for worldly ends; its migration report ties recompense to the migrant's aim. Abū Ḥayyān reports both migration and the warning that afterlife deeds sought for the world yield no afterlife share. Al-Wāḥidī applies the rebuke to worship or Islam for gain. Al-Ālūsī objects that sinful believers cannot thereby be assigned everlasting Hell. Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that importing the deeds restriction from Hūd 11:15–16 confuses recompense for acts with ultimate life goals."}, {"id": "17:18/q01/p3", "position": "The verse classifies a person's ultimate life goal; worldly work can serve the Hereafter and religious acts can serve the world.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the world can be a route to afterlife happiness and notes degrees of attachment and denial; he rejects making the verse a rule for each separate act. Kur'an Yolu likewise distinguishes aim from the kind of work."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q02", "question": "What does ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective names worldly life itself or also the goods and aims sought within it.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q02/p1", "position": "The present, short-lived worldly life, contrasted with the delayed Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and the commentators gloss it as this world. Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn ʿĀshūr supply the understood 'abode' or 'life'; al-Ṭabrisī explains its name by transience. Al-Ālūsī cites 11:15 for the narrow life sense but prefers the wider sense."}, {"id": "17:18/q02/p2", "position": "The world together with its immediate aims, gains, pleasure, or adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers this breadth, citing 42:20, 11:15, and 3:145. Islahi includes immediate gains. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports transient goods or blessings as alternative glosses and explains pleasure sought as an independent end."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q03", "question": "What noun is understood with the adjective ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q03/p1", "position": "An omitted noun such as the immediate abode or worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī supply 'abode'; Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī favor 'life' from the contrast with the Hereafter, and Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 11:15."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q04", "question": "What force do كَانَ and the present يُرِيدُ have here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q04/p1", "position": "They portray continuing or renewed desire for this world.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says kāna adds continuing or exclusive desire and rejects a merely inward resolve or an equally mixed desire. Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes persistent devotion and cites 53:29–30. Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts recurring worldly desire in the present with settled afterlife desire in the past and the omitted kāna; al-Sāmarrāʾī compares repeated and nonrepeated conditions at 31:12 and 4:92–93."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q05", "question": "What worldly thing is hastened, and how much is received?", "turns_on": "Whether 'what We will' specifies God's selected amount alone or may identify the servant's desired object under divine permission.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q05/p1", "position": "God grants only a chosen share of worldly provision or enjoyment, sometimes plenty, little, hardship, or none.", "reasons": "Muqātil names wealth. Al-Farrāʾ names provision. Ṭabarī includes ease, hardship, and chastisement; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, and Ibn al-Jawzī include expansion and restriction, with al-Baghawī also naming destruction. Al-Kashshāf notes some obtain less than sought and some nothing; al-Biqāʿī and al-Bursawī describe loss in both worlds. Al-Bayḍāwī says achievement and concern are gifts; al-Bursawī invokes wisdom. Islahi connects selective gifts with divine respite. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says causal conditions limit the grant, citing 43:33–35 to show wealth has no afterlife worth."}, {"id": "17:18/q05/p2", "position": "The hastened thing is the particular worldly thing the servant wants, insofar as God wills to give it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj allows an implied servant as the subject of 'wishes,' conditional on God's will; al-Kashshāf likewise says the servant's wish may name the thing granted while God determines its recipient."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q06", "question": "How is نَشَآءُ read, and whose wish can it express?", "turns_on": "The transmitted nūn/yāʾ reading and whether the third-person subject is God or the recipient.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q06/p1", "position": "The majority read nashāʾ, 'We will,' making God the speaker and giver.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān identify the majority reading. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says its object can be what God or the seeker wishes, while 'for whom We will' qualifies either."}, {"id": "17:18/q06/p2", "position": "Nāfiʿ also transmits yashāʾ, 'he wills,' with the pronoun referring to God.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī say its sense then matches the common reading; Abū Ḥayyān describes a shift in person."}, {"id": "17:18/q06/p3", "position": "The variant yashāʾ can instead make the seeker or recipient the one who wishes.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports the servant interpretation of the implied subject. Al-Kashshāf says the desired worldly object may be granted to one selected by God; Abū Ḥayyān cautions this is not universal. Al-Ālūsī suggests successful recipients may be enticed by the grant."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q07", "question": "Who is meant by لِمَن نُّرِيدُ?", "turns_on": "Whether 'intend' simply selects a beneficiary or implies that person's destruction; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī say the wording does not bear the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q07/p1", "position": "Only those worldly seekers whom God chooses to receive a worldly grant.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī calls this a restriction to a person God specifically grants. Ibn al-Jawzī reports 'one for whom God intends to hasten something.'"}, {"id": "17:18/q07/p2", "position": "Those whose destruction God intends.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī is reported by Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Ibn al-Jawzī. {"id": "17:18/q09", "question": "What is the syntax of the conditional opening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q09/p1", "position": "مَن is conditional, and عَجَّلْنَا is its response, with مَا as the object.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn also parses لِمَن نُرِيدُ as a partitive apposition with its governing preposition repeated."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q10", "question": "What happens to the worldly seeker after the worldly grant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q10/p1", "position": "God assigns the seeker Hell, where the person enters or suffers it in disgrace and expulsion.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī places this at resurrection and connects blame with ingratitude and misconduct toward favors. Al-Ālūsī reports his definition and infers everlasting Hell for the unbeliever. Asad notes the literal force of assigning Hell. Al-Bursawī says Hell replaces the hoped-for accelerated gift."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q11", "question": "Why is Hell assigned despite a worldly grant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q11/p1", "position": "Worldly gain is no sign of divine approval or afterlife reward; the seeker failed to intend God and chose fleeting life.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq say deeds without intention toward God explain Hell. {"id": "17:18/q12", "question": "How are جَعَلْنَا and يَصْلَىٰهَا construed?", "turns_on": "Whether جَعَلَ needs a supplied second object and whether the circumstantial clause attaches to the person or Hell.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q12/p1", "position": "جَعَلْنَا makes Hell the person's destination or recompense, with a second object understood.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān states Hell is the first object and reports another grammarian supplying an omitted second object. Al-Ālūsī rejects the need to posit that ellipsis."}, {"id": "17:18/q12/p2", "position": "No omitted second object after جَعَلْنَا is required.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects supplying 'destination' or 'recompense.'"}, {"id": "17:18/q12/p3", "position": "يَصْلَىٰهَا is a circumstantial clause about the recipient.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ attaches it to the pronoun in لَهُ; al-Samīn also allows this, and says مَذْمُومًا describes the subject of يَصْلَىٰهَا."}, {"id": "17:18/q12/p4", "position": "يَصْلَىٰهَا is a circumstantial clause about Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī calls it circumstantial; Abū Ḥayyān makes it a circumstance of Hell as first object of جَعَلْنَا; al-Samīn permits either attachment."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q13", "question": "What does يَصْلَىٰهَا mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb emphasizes enduring heat or entering the fire; the cited lexicon distinguishes related forms.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q13/p1", "position": "To endure Hell's heat.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl gives the heat gloss. The lexicon cited by Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains ṣaly as kindling or enduring fire's heat."}, {"id": "17:18/q13/p2", "position": "To enter Hell, or be caused to enter it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports entry as another gloss. The cited lexicon distinguishes ṣallā, entering, from aṣlā, causing someone to enter."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q14", "question": "What does مَذْمُومًا express?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q14/p1", "position": "Blamed, reproached, or disgraced, including blame amid divine punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses blameworthiness. Al-Zajjāj equates it with مذءوم. Qatāda places blame in punishment and amid God's favor; Ṭabarī names ingratitude and bad treatment of favors. Abū Ḥayyān stresses humiliation."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q15", "question": "What does مَّدْحُورًا mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q15/p1", "position": "Expelled or driven far away, especially from God's mercy and Paradise.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites دحر and repelling Satan, with verbal noun الدحور. Yaḥyā specifies exile from Paradise into Hell; Qatāda speaks of torment. Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī connect it to removal from mercy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds disgrace, humiliation, and displeasure; the cited Majmaʿ lexicon says expulsion and distance."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q16", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this warning?", "turns_on": "The reports name different groups; al-Ālūsī tests the campaign report against the sūra's Meccan revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q16/p1", "position": "It was said to concern three men of Thaqīf.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Farqad ibn Yamāma, Abū Fāṭima ibn al-Bukhturī, and Ṣafwān, then adds two unnamed placeholders."}, {"id": "17:18/q16/p2", "position": "It concerned emigrants seeking booty instead of God's reward.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this without naming the emigrants."}, {"id": "17:18/q16/p3", "position": "It concerned hypocrites joining Muslim campaigns for booty rather than religious reward.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān report it; al-Ālūsī rejects this occasion because the sūra is Meccan and this verse is not among its exceptions, while adding that general wording outruns any specific occasion."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q17", "question": "How do this verse and related teachings distinguish worldly and afterlife aims?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse primarily classifies ultimate life goals or supplies a rule for the acceptance of each mixed-motive deed.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q17/p1", "position": "The intended end governs a deed's value; an apparently pious deed may seek worldly reward, while worldly activity may serve the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān cite migration for a worldly prize or woman and fighting for gain. Al-Burhān and Kur'an Yolu connect the contrast to the hadith that actions depend on intentions. Al-Rāzī classifies pursuit of this world, the Hereafter, both, or neither. Al-Wāḥidī rebukes professed Islam for worldly gain; al-Ṭabrisī says it receives no afterlife reward."}, {"id": "17:18/q17/p2", "position": "Mixed motives form further classes; scholars differ over accepting an act when afterlife intent dominates, but reject it when worldly intent dominates or ties.", "reasons": "A discussion reported by Ṭabāṭabāʾī from Rūḥ al-maʿānī divides agents into four classes and mixed motives by predominance. Its fourth class, a voluntary act with neither motive, is impossible to those who require every act to have a motive; others call it inwardly ineffective yet outwardly forbidden. Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects applying this act-by-act taxonomy to verses about a person's ultimate life-goal."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q18", "question": "How does the verse connect with its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "How the conditional worldly promise relates to adjacent accountability and more general statements of worldly reward.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q18/p1", "position": "It contrasts the worldly seeker's uncertain allotment and fate with afterlife seeking, as part of the passage's account of divine judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Qaffāl and the Rāzī reading cited by Kur'an Yolu link it to 17:13 and personal responsibility: rejecting prophets for status makes one's deeds lead to Hell. Ibn ʿĀshūr draws the sole-world restriction from the next sentence. Ṭabāṭabāʾī places it after worldly destruction of nations and says afterlife effort is thanked while worldly provision depends on divine choice. Islahi situates the section's warning to Jews and Quraysh about rejection, signs, and national punishment; Study Quran notes earthly and afterlife warnings as sūra themes."}, {"id": "17:18/q18/p2", "position": "Other verses describe worldly recompense more generally, while this verse qualifies its amount and recipient.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites 3:145 for worldly reward. Ibn Kathīr says the double restriction qualifies more general promises. Al-Qurṭubī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī discuss Hūd 11:15–16; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it concerns recompense for deeds rather than this verse's life-goal contrast. Al-Rāzī invokes 18:104 for worldly losers who suppose they do well."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q19", "question": "What inward account is given of the worldly seeker and Hell?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q19/p1", "position": "Attachment to nature and appetite clouds spiritual readiness; Hell images deprivation and expulsion from mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī invokes the allotted share in the Preserved Tablet and describes Hell as a dark well of nature, its fire as deprivation and its blame in both worlds. Al-Ālūsī describes a turbid disposition overwhelmed by desire. Al-Wāsiṭī says witnessing the Hereafter accompanies renouncing the world, divine support effaces self-regard, and contemplating divine attributes causes servant attributes to fall away."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q20", "question": "Was a broader promise of full worldly gain abrogated by this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q20/p1", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās says the earlier promise of full health, family joy, money, and children was abrogated by 17:18.", "reasons": "The report glosses the desired life as its reward and its adornment as wealth, then treats this verse's restriction as the abrogating rule."}]}

ounced.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q21/p1", "position": "Assimilation is transmitted and practiced by most performance authorities.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports it across Ibn Farḥ's routes from al-Dūrī and Ibn Jarīr's from al-Sūsī, as read by al-Dānī and his students. {"id": "17:18/q22", "question": "What ancillary grammatical parsing is cited alongside 17:18?", "turns_on": "Whether idhā is governed as a genitive or remains adverbial in the cited cross-reference.", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q22/p1", "position": "Al-Akhfash takes idhā as genitive under ḥattā.", "reasons": "The citation concerns an idhā construction that the note associates with 17:18."}, {"id": "17:18/q22/p2", "position": "Most grammarians keep idhā adverbial; ḥattā introduces the full clause, and the second idhā apposes the first.", "reasons": "They infer an omitted response for the first idhā, namely people dividing into three groups, and cite 56:7–8; the note also references 17:18."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q23", "question": "Does the written form of مَا نَشَآءُ differ in the codex?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q23/p1", "position": "A parallel occurrence in Shuʿayb's verse has an extra written wāw, without a change in meaning.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says the codex writes ما نشؤا there with wāw after alif, whereas the same form elsewhere lacks it."}]}
{"id": "17:18/q24", "question": "What can attachment to the world do to a person's judgment and obedience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:18/q24/p1", "position": "It can obscure obedience and reflect a mistaken estimate of worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says God deals with people according to knowledge of inner good and evil, while attachment to leadership, wealth, and pleasure can prevent obedience to messengers. {"id": "17:19/q01", "question": "What is the Hereafter sought here?", "turns_on": "Whether desire names the ultimate life sought or is restricted to seeking its reward through particular deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q01/p1", "position": "Paradise, its abode and delights, or its reward and good.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names Paradise; al-Wāḥidī also reports reward or good of the Hereafter and compares 3:145. {"id": "17:19/q02", "question": "What does seeking the Hereafter require as an intention?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is applied to the motive of each deed, a person's governing life-goal, or an inward predisposition.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q02/p1", "position": "Making the Hereafter one's sincere aim is necessary for deeds to benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī invokes 53:39 and the saying on intentions, explaining that worship must be intended to illuminate the heart through knowledge and love of God. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī infer intention and sincerity from the lām. Al-Burhān cites the contrast with 17:18 and verses on intended hearts and bound oaths. Kuran Yolu and Study Quran cite the prophetic saying on intentions, including emigration for God versus marriage or worldly benefit; the latter says an earnest attempt need not succeed or be completed. Abū Ḥafṣ excludes ostentation, reputation, self-regard and even desire for compensation."}, {"id": "17:19/q02/p2", "position": "The aim is a settled orientation toward the next life; ordinary worldly work can serve it.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu says honest worldly work done under God's rules, with accountability and hope of reward, can seek the Hereafter, while apparent worship can seek worldly gain. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the verses classify ultimate life-goals, not acceptance of each individual act. Al-Kashshāf depicts the believer choosing afterlife riches and accepting worldly poverty."}, {"id": "17:19/q02/p3", "position": "Genuine desire arises from a sound spiritual readiness and seeks latent perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the desired perfection is potentially present in the decree and effort brings it into actuality; al-Ālūsī likewise describes a clear disposition and sound nature."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q03", "question": "Why is desire for the Hereafter expressed in the past tense?", "turns_on": "Whether the past tense emphasizes the seeker's settled state or the singularity of the desired Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q03/p1", "position": "It portrays afterlife desire as settled, unlike renewed worldly desire.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts the past and omitted kāna here with the present tense of worldly desire in 17:18."}, {"id": "17:19/q03/p2", "position": "Desire for the one Hereafter is a single act, unlike recurrent desires for reward with each deed.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares 3:145; he generally says present conditional verbs mark recurrence and past verbs mark actions that do not or should not recur, comparing gratitude and disbelief and accidental and deliberate killing."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q04", "question": "What does saʿy mean?", "turns_on": "The literal motion sense and its extended sense of purposeful deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q04/p1", "position": "Effort, work, or action, especially deeds toward the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Dāmghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī give the sense of work or deeds; al-Dāmghānī compares 92:4, 22:51 and 34:5. Al-Ālūsī says it often denotes exertion in good deeds and cites a line by ʿAlqama ibn Saʿd."}, {"id": "17:19/q04/p2", "position": "Literally brisk walking, slower than running; figuratively earnest striving toward good or evil.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports al-Rāghib's lexical definition. Al-Ālūsī similarly gives brisk walking, while Ibn ʿĀshūr says walking rather than running and compares good works to a traveler's route to the Hereafter."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q05", "question": "What kind of effort is due to the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "The notes describe either prescribed outward deeds or the corresponding inward mode of striving.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q05/p1", "position": "The fitting effort is sustained lawful good deeds: doing what God commands and avoiding what He forbids.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī specify obedience pleasing to God; Ibn ʿAbbās names obligations and God's rights. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds good speech under the law; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī exclude invented devotions. Ibn Kathīr names following the Messenger. Al-Biqāʿī names Book and Sunna, requiring action when possible and capacity when action is not. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī requires full effort grounded in certain reason or legal proof. Ibn ʿĀshūr says wishing without the path is self-deception, citing Ibn al-Mubārak's poem about a ship sailing on dry land. Al-Rāzī rejects star or angel intermediaries, images of prophets or saints, and self-killing or burning as invalid devotional paths."}, {"id": "17:19/q05/p2", "position": "The effort has inward forms: the heart strives toward the Hereafter and aspiration strives toward God.", "reasons": "Some authorities reported by al-Sulamī and al-Ālūsī distinguish bodily striving for worldly life, heart-striving for the Hereafter, and spiritual aspiration toward God. Al-Bursawī describes the lower self inclining to Hell, the spirit to Paradise, and the heart turning by wrath or grace; grace turns it sincerely toward God. Al-Qāshānī makes effort actualize a perfection already latent."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q06", "question": "How is سعيها parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative is the verb's object or a cognate accusative specifying its kind.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q06/p1", "position": "A direct object: the deeds appropriate to the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this as one parse; al-Nasafī reports direct striving toward the Hereafter. Al-Ṭabarī identifies the feminine pronoun as referring to the Hereafter."}, {"id": "17:19/q06/p2", "position": "A cognate or absolute accusative specifying the kind of striving, with لها meaning for its sake.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the cognate accusative analysis; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the possessive a verbal noun semantically related to its object and the accusative one specifying kind. eking and effort?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q08/p1", "position": "Sound, enduring faith is indispensable; it includes God's oneness, revelation and messengers, and belief in requital.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses oneness; al-Ṭabarī reward; Ibn ʿAṭiyya certainty about God, the Hereafter and His messages; al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī reject association and denial. {"id": "17:19/q09", "question": "What conditions together make effort accepted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q09/p1", "position": "Afterlife intention, sound or prescribed action, and firm faith must come together.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī transmit an early threefold saying: firm faith, sincere intent, correct action. {"id": "17:19/q10", "question": "Are deeds with mixed worldly and afterlife motives accepted?", "turns_on": "Whether a dominant afterlife motive preserves sincerity, and whether this verse addresses individual deeds at all.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q10/p1", "position": "Any worldly association spoils the deed, even when afterlife intent predominates.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports a divine saying rejecting works with association and an analysis that mixed motives defeat purity; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the same debate from Rūḥ al-maʿānī."}, {"id": "17:19/q10/p2", "position": "A deed can be accepted when afterlife intent predominates.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this alternative; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the disagreement over the dominant afterlife motive."}, {"id": "17:19/q10/p3", "position": "A deed is unaccepted if worldly motive predominates or ties with afterlife motive.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls this agreed, though he deems such a deed better than seeking worldly gain alone; the discussion reported by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also calls it agreed."}, {"id": "17:19/q10/p4", "position": "The verse classifies people's ultimate goals, not the acceptance of every mixed-motive deed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the reported application to individual acts and says the world is either the end or a stage to the Hereafter."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q11", "question": "Can a voluntary deed have no motive, and what follows?", "turns_on": "Whether a motive is necessary for any voluntary act.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q11/p1", "position": "A voluntary deed without a motive is impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and the discussion quoted by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī attribute this to those who hold that every voluntary act requires a motive."}, {"id": "17:19/q11/p2", "position": "Such an act is possible but inwardly ineffective and outwardly forbidden as pointless.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and the discussion quoted by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī attribute this to those who do not require a motive."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q12", "question": "What is the grammatical force of وهو مؤمن?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q12/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial nominal clause describing the seeker during the effort, with faith shown as stable and accompanying desire and action.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn identifies the subject of سعى as the clause's referent. {"id": "17:19/q13", "question": "Who does أولئك denote, and why is it plural?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q13/p1", "position": "It denotes the previously described seekers; the plural follows the collective meaning of singular من.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explains the shift from singular relative to plural demonstrative. {"id": "17:19/q14", "question": "What does their final سعي refer back to?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun resumes all preceding qualifications or only the explicit striving.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q14/p1", "position": "All the qualifying deeds and conditions just described.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this scope as one reading."}, {"id": "17:19/q14/p2", "position": "The effort specifically named earlier, whose central place the wording highlights.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this narrower scope and its emphasis."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q15", "question": "What does God thanking the effort mean?", "turns_on": "Whether thanks is expressed as general acceptance and praise, specific multiplied reward and pardon, or attaining the inward goal.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q15/p1", "position": "God accepts, praises and rewards the effort and its doer, including Paradise.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā name Paradise; al-Suddī names repayment. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the report of a man forgiven after giving water to a thirsty dog."}, {"id": "17:19/q15/p3", "position": "God grants the sought object through the seeker's realized spiritual readiness.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says sound original nature, faith and works bring the sought perfection from potentiality into actuality; al-Bursawī describes grace turning the heart upward until it finds God."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q16", "question": "Why is kāna used with مشكورا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q16/p1", "position": "It shows that their effort was already worthy of thanks in worldly life, before later reward.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes its present worthiness from the ensuing recompense."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q17", "question": "For whom was the verse revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q17/p1", "position": "Bilāl the muezzin and others.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports this occasion without specifying the others."}]}
{"id": "17:19/q18", "question": "What does the contrast with the worldly seeker teach?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different, compatible implications from the contrast and its wider context.", "positions": [{"id": "17:19/q18/p1", "position": "Seeking the Hereafter succeeds and can include worldly good; seeking only this world may achieve neither.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī's report from al-Ḥasan make this contrast; al-Iṣlāḥī says afterlife seekers receive their ordained worldly share.
